forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Milton Keynes forecasts a £0.376m high needs deficit by the end of 2026/27
news_drafts.lead:
Milton Keynes Council forecasts a deficit of £0.376m at the end of 2026/27 on high needs, the part of the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) that pays for children with special educational needs and disabilities. Its second-quarter forecast outturn report says the block "remains under significant pressure". The Budget and Resources Scrutiny Committee meets on 2 December.

The report gives an in-year overspend of £1.6m on high needs, partly offset by reserves of £1.2m. It records 87 independent placements against a budget of 80. The overall schools grant surplus carried forward is £1.623m against £2.514m budgeted, an adverse movement of £0.891m that the report says is driven mainly by the Early Years block. The council's SEND Reform Plan is awaiting approval from the Department for Education, expected in November.

The reserves risk assessment for the draft 2027/28 budget says the council is "anticipating that it will go into deficit in 2026/27 and that this will increase further in 2027/28". It gives a maximum of £64.7m for the high needs deficit and holds a £1m risk provision. It says the council is liable for any high needs shortfall against national funding, and that it is seeking to reduce the deficit through budget reductions, reform and a transfer from the schools block, which needs the department's approval. The General Fund annex says the effect on the General Fund is "currently unclear" while the council awaits government announcements on financial support.

news_drafts.headline: Milton Keynes forecasts £0.376m high needs deficit for 2026/27, and £2.473m schools grant deficit for 2027/28
news_drafts.lead:
Milton Keynes City Council forecasts a deficit of £0.376m on high needs, the part of schools funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, at the end of 2026/27. Its draft 2027/28 budget, before Cabinet on 1 December, forecasts a year-end deficit of £2.473m on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools. The Department for Education (DfE) has not yet confirmed allocations for 2027/28.

The 2026/27 figure comes from the period 6 forecast: an in-year high needs deficit of £1.615m, partly offset by a £1.239m surplus brought forward. The papers say high needs funding rose by 0% in 2026/27, which created pressure on the budget. The council received nothing from the High Needs Stability Grant, which paid £5.812bn nationally in October at 90% of each authority's deficit at 31 March 2026, because it held a surplus then. The quarter 2 report forecasts the grant's carry-forward at £1.623m against £2.514m budgeted, mainly from an Early Years DfE adjustment and additional provider payments.

The council's High Needs Block Action Plan "has delivered substantial savings to date", the paper says, with no figure given. Schools Forum did not approve moving 0.5% of the schools block, about £1.515m, to high needs, so the council has asked the DfE to approve the transfer. The outcome will be reported in the Final Budget report.

news_drafts.headline: Milton Keynes used all its remaining schools surplus to balance 2026/27, and expects a high needs deficit
news_drafts.lead:
Milton Keynes City Council used all of its remaining brought-forward surplus on special educational needs funding to balance the 2026/27 budget, and expects to start 2027/28 in deficit on that spending, papers for the Budget and Resources Scrutiny Committee on 6 October show. The money is in the "high needs" block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, paid for from the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools).

The council's medium-term financial outlook says costs on high needs are running ahead of government funding. It says "there is a chance that the block will go into a deficit during the 2026/27 if there were to be any in year overspend", so "it is therefore likely we may start the 2027/28 financial year in a deficit." A separate General Fund annex, covering the council's main day-to-day budget, says the block "is expected to go into Deficit in 2026/27". It says the effect on that budget is unclear "as we await Government announcements on whether there will be any financial support." The paper gives no figure for the deficit. A review with the high needs school reference group is under way to find savings.

A statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps such deficits off a council's main balance sheet, lets them be carried forward until 2028. The paper estimates councils with schools responsibilities hold about £5 billion of high needs deficits between them by the end of 2025/26. The council also says it will not receive its indicative 2027/28 schools funding until December 2026. Draft allocations "used to be published in July", it says, and this is the third year of delay. The full budget update will wait until then.

findings.headline: Total pressures are shown as £7,407k in 2027/28, £5,237k in 2028/29, £7,793k in 2029/30 and £8,724k in 2030/31.
findings.detail: The risk-level table totals the pressures by year. The demand subtotal (£6,451k) and other subtotal (£733k) for 2027/28 add to £7,184k, not the £7,407k total shown in the same paper.
findings.matters: A council's total pressure across the MTFP is the figure a finance director and lender would use to size the gap, so the difference between subtotals and total is worth checking.

findings.headline: Environmental Services contract annual leave alignment is estimated at £310k from 2027/28, subject to a 15 December delegated decision.
findings.detail: The paper says the council is seeking to align annual leave entitlements across TUPE-transferred staff as part of a proposed contract extension. The final amount depends on agreement with the contractor and confirmation of the affected workforce.
findings.matters: A TUPE-driven contract cost decided by delegation within weeks is a decision point other councils with similar contracts may face.
findings.figures: estimated recurring cost £310k from 2027/28; delegated decision date 15 December
findings.quote: The estimated recurring contract cost is £310k from 2027/28.

findings.headline: Local elections move to a base budget from 2028/29, with a £460k cost and a reserve to smooth the four-year cycle.
findings.detail: The paper says a base budget for average election costs will replace one-off funding from 2028/29. In the fallow year the budget is added to a reserve, which is drawn down when election costs exceed the base budget.
findings.matters: Moving a cyclical cost into a base budget with a reserve is an approach other councils with four-year election cycles may consider.
findings.quote: During this fallow year, the budget will be added to the reserve, which can be drawn down when election costs exceed the base budget.

findings.headline: A £300k saving from charging for second and third food and garden waste bins is reversed after uptake fell short of assumptions.
findings.detail: The paper says demand has been materially below the level assumed in the budget. The income target is reversed, with a corresponding £300k reduction in the Environmental Services contract budget proposed separately.
findings.matters: A charged garden waste service that has not reached the assumed uptake is a saving other councils have also budgeted, and the paper shows how one council reversed it.
findings.figures: £300k saving reversed; corresponding £300k reduction in Environmental Services contract budget; income line -£380k (gross)
findings.quote: Demand has been materially below the level assumed and there is currently insufficient evidence that uptake will increase to the level required.

findings.headline: Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park contract forecast retains the existing £1.9m pressure and adds £500k.
findings.detail: The paper says the council has procured and mobilised a new 10 + 5 year contract for the Waste Recovery Park. The pressure is based on visible operating costs, and any later evidenced efficiency will be reflected in future MTFP updates.
findings.matters: A contract pressure rising by £500k after mobilisation shows how operating costs can move after a re-procurement, which other councils with similar contracts may face.
findings.quote: The current forecast requires the existing £1.9m pressure to be retained and a further £500k added.

daily_post.headline: Milton Keynes' 2027/28 council tax base is 103,062.64 Band D equivalent properties, up from 101,826.87 in 2026/27.
daily_post.lead: The tax base multiplied by the Band D charge sets the council tax income the council can budget for, so a larger base in 2027/28 changes the income assumption in its budget.
